title: Children and Their Parents' Labor Supply: Evidence from Exogenous Variation in Family Size
research_question: What is the causal effect of having an additional child on parents' labor supply outcomes, including employment, hours worked, weeks worked, and earnings? How do these effects differ between mothers and fathers, and across demographic groups such as married versus unmarried women and women with different levels of education?
data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Census Public Use Micro Samples (PUMS), primarily the 1980 and 1990 censuses, focusing on married women (and their husbands) aged 21-35 with at least two children, where the oldest child is less than 18 years old. Key variables include the number of children ever born, sex composition of the first two children, twin births at second parity, maternal age, age at first birth, race/ethnicity, education, and labor market outcomes such as employment status, weeks worked per year, hours worked per week, and labor earnings. The unit of observation is the individual mother (or father). Supplementary 1980 Census samples are used for analyses involving twins.
institutional_context: In post-war U.S. families, fertility decisions are closely tied to women's labor force participation, but disentangling causality is complicated because family size and work decisions are jointly determined by unobserved preferences and constraints. Two features of family formation generate quasi-random variation in family size beyond two children. First, many American parents exhibit a preference for a mixed sibling-sex composition, so couples whose first two children share the same sex are more likely to have a third child. Second, the occurrence of a multiple birth at the second pregnancy unexpectedly increases family size. These features arise from biological chance and parental preferences over sibling composition rather than from labor market conditions, making them useful sources of variation for studying how additional children affect parental work outcomes.

main_estimate.unit: percentage point reduction in labor force participation per additional child (2SLS, same-sex instrument)
main_estimate.interpretation: Having a third child (instrumented by same-sex composition) reduces maternal labor force participation by approximately 12 percentage points — substantially larger than the OLS estimate of ~6pp

secondary_estimate.unit: weeks per year reduction in weeks worked (2SLS)
secondary_estimate.interpretation: An additional child reduces mothers' annual weeks worked by approximately 5 weeks, representing a substantial labor supply withdrawal

public_sources: U.S. Census PUMS 1980 and 1990 (IPUMS USA — free)
Angrist data archive (replication files — free from MIT)
data_availability.proxy_strategy: All data is publicly available through IPUMS USA. Census microdata is free.
data_availability.replicability: high — Census PUMS data freely available from IPUMS; large sample sizes ensure precise replication
data_availability.replication_tier: full (Census PUMS via IPUMS — free; replication code available)
data_availability.data_limitations: Census data is cross-sectional (no panel tracking of individuals over time). Labor supply is measured at a point in time, not dynamically. Sample restricted to married women with at least two children, limiting generalizability to single mothers or women with fewer children.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Instrumental variables — same-sex composition of the first two children as instrument for having a third (or more) child; first stage: same-sex → probability of having ≥3 children; second stage: number of children (instrumented) → maternal labor supply

key_variables.treatment: number of children (endogenous, specifically having a third or higher-order child), instrumented by same-sex composition of first two children
key_variables.control: N/A (continuous/binary treatment with IV; comparison is between families with same-sex vs. mixed-sex first two children)
key_variables.outcome: maternal labor force participation, weeks worked per year, hours worked per week, labor income

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Having more than two children significantly reduces maternal labor supply. The IV estimates show that a third child reduces maternal labor force participation by approximately 10-12 percentage points, weeks worked by approximately 4-6 weeks per year, and labor income by approximately 15-20%. The effect is larger than OLS estimates, suggesting that OLS is biased toward zero by selection (women who have more children would have worked less anyway). Effects on fathers' labor supply are small and statistically insignificant.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Having a third child reduces maternal labor force participation by approximately 10-12 percentage points (2SLS) and weeks worked by approximately 4-6 weeks per year; father's labor supply is essentially unaffected
key_robustness: Twins at second birth as alternative instrument
Comparing same-sex boys (BB) vs. same-sex girls (GG) — both generate similar first stages
Overidentification test using both instruments simultaneously
Controlling for age at first birth and spacing between children

identification_strategy_detail.method: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) with same-sex first two children as instrument for having ≥3 children
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Having three or more children (binary, endogenous), instrumented by same-sex indicator for first two children
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Married woman aged 21-35 with at least two children
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Exclusion restriction: the sex composition of children affects parents' labor supply only through its effect on the number of children (family size), not through direct effects. Potential violations: sex-specific childrearing costs, gender preferences in different cultural groups. The sex of a child is approximately random (50/50), so the instrument satisfies relevance and exogeneity conditions.

key_magnitudes.first_stage: Same-sex first two children increases probability of having ≥3 children by approximately 6 percentage points (F-statistic well above 10)
key_magnitudes.lfp_effect: -10 to -12 percentage points reduction in maternal labor force participation per additional child (2SLS)
key_magnitudes.weeks_effect: -4 to -6 weeks reduction in annual weeks worked
key_magnitudes.income_effect: -15 to -20% reduction in maternal labor income
key_magnitudes.father_effect: Small, positive, and generally insignificant effects on fathers' labor supply

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: The same-sex instrument and twins instrument yield similar 2SLS estimates, supporting the exclusion restriction. Overidentification test does not reject. Results are consistent across 1980 and 1990 Census data. Effects are larger for less-educated mothers, consistent with higher opportunity costs of childcare for lower-wage workers. The BB (two boys) and GG (two girls) indicators have similar first-stage effects, ruling out sex-specific alternative channels.
